The first photograph ever taken required an 8-hour exposure. Joseph Nicéphore Niépce captured it from his window in 1826.
The word 'photography' comes from the Greek words for light (phos) and drawing (graphé) — literally 'drawing with light.'
Kodak's name was invented by George Eastman. He wanted a word that started and ended with 'K' because he thought it was a strong letter.
The most viewed photograph in history is the Windows XP default wallpaper 'Bliss,' shot by Charles O'Rear in Sonoma County, California.
Before digital sensors, a single roll of 35mm film could hold only 36 exposures.
The first color photograph was taken in 1861 by James Clerk Maxwell, the physicist who also unified electromagnetism.
Ansel Adams was originally trained as a concert pianist before dedicating his life to landscape photography.
The 'golden hour' — the period shortly after sunrise or before sunset — produces warm, diffused light prized by photographers worldwide.
Dorothea Lange's 'Migrant Mother' (1936) became the defining image of the Great Depression. The subject, Florence Owens Thompson, was 32.
A camera obscura — a dark room with a small hole projecting an inverted image — was described by Chinese philosopher Mozi around 400 BCE.
The first aerial photograph was taken from a hot air balloon over Paris in 1858 by Nadar (Gaspard-Félix Tournachon).
Henri Cartier-Bresson, father of street photography, called the perfect moment of capture 'the decisive moment.'
The human eye has a dynamic range of about 20 stops of light. The best modern cameras capture around 14-15 stops.
Photojournalism ethics codes prohibit staging, manipulation, and misrepresentation — principles at the heart of Four Corners metadata.
The first press photograph was published in the New York Daily Graphic on March 4, 1880.
Film speed (ISO) was originally called ASA. ISO 400 film was considered 'fast' — modern digital cameras can shoot at ISO 102,400+.
The rule of thirds divides a frame into a 3×3 grid. Placing subjects at intersections creates more dynamic compositions.
Robert Capa's famous advice to photographers: 'If your pictures aren't good enough, you're not close enough.'
The daguerreotype process (1839) used silver-plated copper sheets and mercury vapor. Exposure times were 15-30 minutes.
EXIF data — the metadata embedded in digital photos — can include GPS coordinates, camera settings, and timestamps.
The Four Corners framework ensures photographic context is never separated from the image it describes.
War photographer Don McCullin carried a Nikon F with him in Vietnam. A bullet once hit the camera instead of his chest.
Pinhole cameras have infinite depth of field — everything from inches to infinity is in focus.
The 'Nadar' portraits of 1850s Paris are among the earliest examples of photography used as biographical documentation.
Sebastião Salgado spent 8 years photographing 'Genesis' — pristine landscapes and indigenous peoples across 32 countries.
The first photograph of a human was accidental — a man getting his shoes shined appeared in Daguerre's 1838 Paris boulevard image.
Kodachrome, the iconic color slide film, was discontinued in 2009 after 74 years of production.
A single RAW file from a modern 50-megapixel camera can be over 100 MB — larger than entire early hard drives.
Gordon Parks was the first African American photographer and filmmaker at Life magazine, using his camera as 'a weapon against poverty and racism.'
The Four Corners standard was developed to preserve the chain of custody between a photograph and its contextual metadata.
